PADLAB FIELD GUIDE · BUTTONS & TRIGGERS

Is every button doing its job?

By PadLab · Updated October 5, 2026 · 3 minute read

A controller button test makes missing or stuck inputs easier to spot. Work through each control individually so you can connect a physical press with its on-screen reading.

A complete button check

  1. Open the controller tester and connect your gamepad.
  2. Press each face button slowly and release it. The corresponding cell should show a pressed state and then return to its released value.
  3. Test all four D-pad directions, both shoulder bumpers, the menu controls and each thumbstick click.
  4. Press combinations you use in games. Watch the individual cells while holding and releasing them.
  5. Review the session’s observed-button count. A marked cell means a press was observed, not that the button passed a durability test.

Xbox and PlayStation button equivalents

The standard mapping describes control positions rather than printed symbols. PadLab uses Xbox-style diagram labels and lists PlayStation equivalents in the input cells.

PositionXboxPlayStationStandard index
Bottom face buttonACross0
Right face buttonBCircle1
Left face buttonXSquare2
Top face buttonYTriangle3
Left / right bumperLB / RBL1 / R14 / 5
Left / right triggerLT / RTL2 / R26 / 7

Nintendo face-button lettering differs. For unmapped gamepads, follow numbered buttons and raw axes instead of assuming the standard layout. Extra controls such as touchpads or paddles appear only if the browser exposes them; some duplicate existing inputs.

Test analog trigger travel

Squeeze each trigger gradually. On a standard analog trigger, its value should generally rise from near 0 toward 1, then return when released. Watch for an unexpected jump or a value that stays raised. Some controllers and modes expose triggers as digital buttons, so only two values may be available.

The browser supplies both a numeric value and a pressed flag. A partly squeezed trigger can have a nonzero value before the pressed flag becomes true. PadLab displays both concepts rather than treating every nonzero value as a completed press.

Check vibration separately

If the browser exposes a compatible vibration actuator, Test vibration sends a half-second dual-rumble command. Confirm the physical response yourself. A completed software command is not proof that both motors are healthy, and standard rumble is not a test of DualSense adaptive triggers or every advanced haptic feature.

Understand the limits

A browser can miss very brief transitions between sampled frames. This is not a switch-debounce analyzer or a latency benchmark. If a button behaves differently in a game, check that game's bindings, controller profiles and accessibility settings. For connection problems, use our detection troubleshooting guide.

Reference: MDN: vibration effects and support.
